results.key_finding: Painful tonic spasms are brief, stereotyped, often triggered by movement or touch, and occur with preserved awareness; in this cohort they were more frequent in neuromyelitis optica than in multiple sclerosis, usually after myelitis, and responded to sodium-channel blocking drugs.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS from non-specific white matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 McDonald criteria and excluding neurosarcoidosis, NMOSD and lupus
Do not label the painful tonic spasms as epilepsy or treat them as seizures with antiseizure polytherapy
Do not attribute the hypercalcaemia to MS or ignore it: PTH-independent hypercalcaemia needs its own work-up (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, chest imaging for hilar adenopathy)
Do not start vitamin D supplementation for the low 25-OH vitamin D while the PTH-independent hypercalcaemia is unexplained
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord and right optic nerve, so no separate DIT is required; the two earlier right optic neuritis episodes are prior attacks).

Treat the function-affecting myelitis relapse with high-dose methylprednisolone (IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient, or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days) after excluding urinary infection with a urine dipstick and culture, with glucose monitoring; plasma exchange if the relapse is severe and does not respond.
Assess the worsened bladder urgency with a post-void residual: an antimuscarinic or mirabegron if the residual is low, intermittent self-catheterisation if it is high.

Treat the painful tonic spasms symptomatically with a low-dose sodium-channel blocker such as carbamazepine titrated to effect, checking sodium and blood pressure (carbamazepine induces amlodipine metabolism).

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (three clinical attacks, an enhancing brain lesion and an enhancing thoracic cord lesion, EDSS 3.5: a high-efficacy therapy is appropriate), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before a high-efficacy therapy, screen anti-JCV antibody status (before natalizumab), HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already negative), and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

Source case: 51-year-old woman whose revealing symptom was painful paroxysmal dystonic spasms (right upper limb and hemiface), with prior transient demyelinating episodes (visual blurring, right hemibody paresthesias) resolving spontaneously, multiple supratentorial + cervical demyelinating lesions including an enhancing right centrum semiovale lesion, positive CSF oligoclonal bands, treated with 5-day IV methylprednisolone then fingolimod (relapsing course, EDSS 1 at 15 months). Verified against the source via WebFetch at authoring time. NeuroBench adaptation: age set to 46 (late-onset, within 40-55), Afro-Brazilian ethnicity for batch demographic diversity, painful tonic spasms retained as the instructive atypical paroxysmal symptom, prior visual episodes recast as optic neuritis misdiagnosed as migraine aura, and PTH-independent mild hypercalcemia + low-titer ANA added as authored red herrings (not from the source) to create the moderate-complexity neurosarcoidosis/CNS-lupus rule-out. patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Carvalho is a 46-year-old right-handed Afro-Brazilian secondary school teacher who presents to the neurology service for evaluation of a three-week history of progressive right-sided leg weakness, numbness below the waist, and stereotyped painful muscle contractions in the right arm and leg. Her symptoms began approximately three weeks ago with a tingling, electric sensation in both feet that initially she attributed to prolonged standing at work. Over the following week, she developed right leg weakness that made stair climbing difficult, accompanied by a band-like tightness around her lower chest. She noted that her bladder urgency has worsened over this period, with two near-incontinence episodes. She denies frank urinary retention.

The most distressing symptom has been episodic, intensely painful stiffening of the right arm and leg occurring 4-6 times daily, each lasting 30-90 seconds. These episodes are stereotyped — the right arm flexes at the elbow and the right leg extends — and are sometimes triggered by touching the right arm or by sudden movement. She has no loss of consciousness, no tongue biting, and no postictal confusion during these events. Her husband observed three episodes and confirms they are focal, brief, and do not spread to involve the face or cause loss of awareness.

Four years ago, she experienced two episodes of transient visual blurring in her right eye, each lasting 2-3 weeks, accompanied by mild aching pain behind the right eye. These were attributed to 'atypical migraine with visual aura' by a general neurologist; no MRI brain was obtained at the time, and her vision recovered fully on both occasions. She did not pursue further workup.

Six months ago, routine blood work revealed mild hypercalcemia (10.6 mg/dL). PTH was checked and was not elevated. The cause of the hypercalcemia was not pursued further as the patient was lost to follow-up. She has been on amlodipine for hypertension for three years with good blood pressure control. She is a former smoker (5 pack-years, quit 10 years ago) and has no occupational or environmental exposures to dust, birds, or mold.

The patient denies fevers, weight loss, night sweats, rash, joint swelling, oral ulcers, or lymphadenopathy. She has no prior neurological hospitalizations. Family history is negative for MS or demyelinating disease.

neurological_exam.additional: Lhermitte sign present — patient reports electric shock-like sensation down the spine with neck flexion. Uhthoff phenomenon reported: symptoms worsen after hot showers or during warm weather. Over the past 3 weeks, patient has been experiencing brief, painful muscle contractions lasting 30-90 seconds, predominantly in the right arm and leg, occurring 4-6 times per day, occasionally triggered by movement or touch. She describes these as intensely painful, involuntary stiffening episodes that are stereotyped in character. EDSS estimated at 3.5.
